claim: Cao et al. harness raises pooled accuracy of Sonnet-4.6 from 48.3 to 56.9 across HLE-Verified, LiveCodeBench v6 and R-Bench-V, using a pre-solve feeling-of-knowing (FOK) and post-solve judgment-of-learning (JOL) score to decide retry, stop or aggregate.
quote: Metacognitive Harness 56.9 vs Sonnet-4.6 Pass@1 48.3 overall accuracy (Table 1 Panel B)
title: LLMs Know When They Know, but Do Not Act on It: A Metacognitive Harness for Test-time Scaling
n: 3 benchmarks, 1859 questions, Claude Sonnet-4.6; ablation n=100
transfer: Agent step: ask the model for FOK before solving and JOL after; use them to gate retries.

claim: The paper does report cost. Average cost per question: pass@1 $0.29, Self-Refine $0.45, budget forcing $0.67, verifier reranking $1.32, aggregator (4 attempts) $1.42, harness $0.78 with 2.4 average attempts. So the harness costs about 2.7x pass@1, not equal to it. It is cheaper than 4-attempt aggregation and scored higher (56.9 vs 53.7).
quote: Avg. Inference Cost / Q. reports the total inference cost divided by the number of evaluated questions.
title: LLMs Know When They Know, but Do Not Act on It: A Metacognitive Harness for Test-time Scaling
n: 3 benchmarks, 1859 questions, Claude Sonnet-4.6; ablation n=100
transfer: Compare any metacognitive gate against fixed-K at equal cost, not against a single pass.

claim: Ablation on 100 questions: full harness 47.0 [37,57] at average K 2.58; random retry with matched K 45.7 [43,48] at K 2.58; pass@1 44.0. Confidence intervals overlap heavily, so evidence that FOK/JOL direction beats undirected retries at equal budget is weak.
quote: Random retry and fixed-K variants underperform despite matched or comparable budgets, indicating that the gain does not come simply from more attempts, but from directed exploration.
title: LLMs Know When They Know, but Do Not Act on It: A Metacognitive Harness for Test-time Scaling
n: 3 benchmarks, 1859 questions, Claude Sonnet-4.6; ablation n=100
transfer: Do not credit metacognitive signals until a larger matched-K test separates them from random retry.

claim: Per-benchmark gains are uneven. LiveCodeBench Easy gets -0.7 (95.4 to 94.7), Medium +1.1, Hard +19.6. HLE gets +12.0. Gains concentrate on hard items; on easy single-answer items the harness gives nothing or slightly hurts.
quote: Gain +12.0 +10.0 -0.7 +1.1 +19.6 (HLE, LCB overall, easy, medium, hard)
title: LLMs Know When They Know, but Do Not Act on It: A Metacognitive Harness for Test-time Scaling
n: 3 benchmarks, 1859 questions, Claude Sonnet-4.6; ablation n=100
transfer: Matches our finding: gate extra effort on predicted difficulty, leave easy items at the first answer.

claim: The authors state limits: only Sonnet-4.6 passes all diagnosis checks among nine models; the controller is an SVM fitted on a 100-example anchor set; evaluation is benchmark reasoning, not long-horizon agents.
quote: Our main end-to-end evaluation therefore focuses on Sonnet-4.6, which exhibits the strongest metacognitive diagnosis in our model panel.
title: LLMs Know When They Know, but Do Not Act on It: A Metacognitive Harness for Test-time Scaling
n: 3 benchmarks, 1859 questions, Claude Sonnet-4.6; ablation n=100
transfer: Calibrate FOK/JOL on a small anchor set of our own tasks before trusting them. Re-diagnose when the model changes.

claim: CHECK: The Cao gain is not only extra calls in the authors' own data (harness 56.9 beats the 4-attempt aggregator 53.7 at about half the cost). But the matched-K ablation against random retry is n=100 with overlapping CIs, and no independent replication was found. Verdict: partly settled. Cost data exists (the critique said none). Directed-versus-random advantage is unproven. Tasks are hard reasoning, not open-ended generation.
quote: Panel B compares the proposed metacognitive harness against test-time scaling baselines under matched or comparable inference budgets.
title: LLMs Know When They Know, but Do Not Act on It: A Metacognitive Harness for Test-time Scaling
n: 3 benchmarks, 1859 questions, Claude Sonnet-4.6; ablation n=100
transfer: Treat as a hypothesis; run our own cost-matched test with a random-retry control.

claim: Sinha and Kapur 2021 meta-analysis: 53 studies, 166 comparisons. Problem solving before instruction beat instruction first with Hedges g = 0.36, larger when the design followed productive-failure principles. Grades 2 to 5 and domain-general skills favored instruction first. A publication-bias-corrected g = 0.87 appears in the summary I read; I did not verify it in the paper.
quote: PS-I showed a moderate advantage (Hedges' g = 0.36)
title: When Problem Solving Followed by Instruction Works: Evidence for Productive Failure
transfer: Weak. Humans only. An LLM does not learn from a failed attempt inside one call. Possible step: attempt, then compare to a reference, only where an outside check exists.

claim: CHECK: Sinha and Kapur headline g = 0.36 is confirmed from the Crossref record. The domain-structuredness moderator and the hostile-opinion counterweight were not checked. Do not use the 0.87 bias-corrected figure until the paper is read. Verdict: headline confirmed, moderators unverified. Publisher page gave HTTP 403.
title: When Problem Solving Followed by Instruction Works: Evidence for Productive Failure
venue: Review of Educational Research (via Crossref API)

claim: Rowland 2014 is a single-author meta-analysis in Psychological Bulletin 140(6), 1432-1463, on testing versus restudy. Record confirmed via Europe PMC (PMID 25150680) and Crossref. The abstract with effect sizes could not be retrieved. Reported finding: initial recall tests help more than recognition tests, supporting effortful-processing accounts.
quote: The effect of testing versus restudy on retention: a meta-analytic review of the testing effect.
title: The effect of testing versus restudy on retention: A meta-analytic review of the testing effect
transfer: Low. An LLM does not forget between calls, so retrieval practice has no clear analogue.

claim: CHECK: Rowland g = 0.50 could not be verified (PubMed needs cookies, APA and Sage blocked, Crossref has no abstract). Verdict: still unverified; keep it marked as memory. It is not a design input anyway.
title: Testing effect meta-analysis

claim: Reflexion-style self-reflection is limited by the quality of the self-generated feedback: Self-Contrast reports that this feedback, not the reflection process, is the bottleneck of LLM self-correction. This supports storing lessons only when an external signal exists. It does not directly test lessons going stale.
quote: Our investigation unveils that the key bottleneck is the quality of the self-evaluated feedback.
authors: Zhang, Shen, Wu, Peng, Wang, Zhuang, Lu
title: Self-Contrast: Better Reflection Through Inconsistent Solving Perspectives
transfer: Store lessons only from verified outcomes. Tag each lesson with its evidence and let it expire.

claim: Only indirect evidence on expertise reversal in LLMs: GPT-3.5 used as a judge of educational content reproduced the human expertise reversal effect. That is LLMs simulating learners, not worked examples hurting a strong model. No direct equal-token test was found.
quote: GPT-3.5 judgments reproduced known learning effects, including the Expertise Reversal Effect.
title: Evaluating and Optimizing Educational Content with Large Language Model Judgments
transfer: none directly. Test few-shot against zero-shot on our own easy tasks.

claim: CHECK: The gap 'predict before solving whether a task is open-ended or single-answer' has no direct study found. Web search budget ran out after one query. Cao's FOK is the nearest thing, but it predicts correctness on hard reasoning, not open-endedness. Verdict: unsettled, gap remains.
title: gap check
transfer: Build our own router and measure it on our NoveltyBench and ARC data.

claim: CHECK: Reflexion lesson staleness and expertise reversal in LLMs were not settled. The session web search limit was reached and arXiv API probes returned nothing direct. Verdict: both gaps remain open; rerun when budget refills.
title: gap check
